summary: Microsoft authors translate natural-language contact-center routing rules into executable workflow DAGs (conditional actions, parallel branches, hit-first fallback chains, boolean predicates) in a commercial platform's JSON dialect. They diagnose an 'emission-density bottleneck': models pick the right nodes but mis-wire attributes and boolean grouping as the number of interdependent nodes emitted in one pass grows. The fix is a fixed pipeline: a learned registry selector narrows the vocabulary, the LLM emits a compact intermediate representation (IR), and a deterministic compiler builds the graph. On a 635-rule templated synthetic benchmark, four configurations (Monolithic, Selector->JSON, IR-only, Selector+IR) are run on GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.3-chat (non-reasoning) and GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6 (reasoning references), judged by Opus 4.6. Selector+IR lifts GPT-5.3-chat judge validity by 24.3 pp and reaches TOST equivalence with GPT-5.2 out of the box, at ~0.55x the prompt tokens with 99-100% valid JSON. It does not help GPT-4.1 (-2.2 pp, n.s.), and edge-direction (ordering) errors remain about half of residual failures. Data, schemas and code are proprietary.

claims.claim: With the right neuro-symbolic decomposition, lower-cost non-reasoning LLMs generate complex workflow DAGs at production-relevant quality without reasoning models
claims.evidence: Holds for one of the two non-reasoning models. GPT-5.3-chat Selector+IR vs GPT-5.2 monolithic: +0.8 pp, 90% CI [-2.0, +3.6], TOST p=0.007 at the stated margin; vs Opus 4.6 equivalence only at +/-7. GPT-4.1 Selector+IR 64.6% judge validity vs 66.8% monolithic (-2.2, McNemar n.s.) and fails equivalence until +/-12. An ~8-point frontier gap remains.

claims.claim: Across four models, the full system reaches approximately 89% LLM-judge validity and approximately 90% exact-match condition accuracy (metadata abstract)
claims.evidence: These are best-model maxima, not cross-model results: Table 1 Selector+IR judge validity is 64.6 (GPT-4.1), 80.6 (GPT-5.3-chat), 84.1 (GPT-5.2), 88.8 (Opus 4.6); condition accuracy 78.1 / 82.2 / 89.6 / 88.0. The full-text abstract says 'reaches up to', which is accurate; the arXiv listing abstract drops the qualifier.

claims.claim: Models select the right graph nodes almost perfectly but drop content as the number of interdependent nodes emitted in one pass grows
claims.evidence: Emission-density curve with Wilson 95% bands aggregated over all four models; monolithic accuracy falls to ~55% in the 13-15 condition band while node-set accuracy stays high (App. B, Table 3). Single greedy run; per-band CIs widen at high density.

claims.claim: The IR plus deterministic compiler yields valid output by construction
claims.evidence: IR-only produces zero uncompilable output across all four models with 99-100% valid JSON; one hard failure in 5,080 generations overall. Follows from the compiler design.

claims.claim: The full system uses roughly half the per-rule prompt tokens of a monolithic prompt
claims.evidence: Selector+IR total tokens 0.55-0.56x monolithic across models (Table 2, App. G). Token counts are deterministic; dollar cost and latency are not reported.

claims.claim: Structure does not fix edge-direction (ordering) errors
claims.evidence: Ordering errors are 49.5% of residual failures and barely move across configurations, by keyword-gated error coding (App. E). This is the paper's own negative result.

claims.claim: Splitting generation into plan->expand or code-locked scaffolds consistently failed; decomposition relocates the bottleneck rather than removing it
claims.evidence: Stated as a lesson learned with no configuration, numbers or table.

Blind two-author study on 100 items, kappa=0.82 on a 22-item double-annotated overlap; App. A argues self-preference is limited although Opus 4.6 is also one of the generators. One pinned rulebook for every system.

patterns.note: The system is a fixed three-stage workflow (registry selector -> LLM emits IR -> deterministic compiler builds the DAG). Comparison: same model, same 635 rules, same judge, against a single monolithic prompt. Selector+IR wins clearly on GPT-5.3-chat (+24.3 pp, p<0.001) and modestly on GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.6 (+4.3, +4.7, p<0.05), and gives no gain on GPT-4.1 (-2.2, n.s.) (Table 4). Single greedy run per cell. The alternative is a one-shot prompt, not an agent loop, and the main lever is moving graph assembly into deterministic code, not graph-structured control flow.

The LLM-generated DAG here is the business deliverable (a routing graph), not the agent's own task plan, so the paper does not test task-DAG orchestration. Indirect caution: LLMs mis-wire edges as the count of interdependent nodes grows, ordering errors are 49.5% of residual failures, and §7 reports (without numbers) that plan->expand decomposition failed.

Same-model comparison: Selector+IR uses 0.55-0.56x the tokens of the monolithic prompt while matching or improving validity on 3 of 4 models (Table 2). Vocabulary narrowing via a learned selector is the main token saver.
Selector then generator is a two-stage pipeline, not planner-executor; the plan->expand variant that would test P13 is reported only anecdotally as failing (§7).
Opus 4.6 judge, partially validated (kappa=0.82 on 22 double-coded items); Opus 4.6 is also a generator under test.

methodology.sample: 635 templated synthetic routing rules ('manufactured synthetic data') over scenario families, density up to 15 conditions; no production traffic evaluated
methodology.baselines: Same-model monolithic prompt; Selector->JSON and IR-only ablations; reasoning models out of the box as quality references
methodology.models: GPT-4.1, GPT-5.3-chat (non-reasoning); GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.6 (reasoning references); Opus 4.6 as judge
methodology.variance: Single greedy run per model x config; Wilson 95% CIs, paired McNemar tests and TOST equivalence; per-family marginal CIs about +/-15-25 pp
methodology.ablations: Four configurations isolate the selector and the IR/compiler; plan->expand variant mentioned without data
methodology.contamination_controls: Proprietary synthetic data, not public; contamination unlikely
methodology.languages: JSON dialect of a commercial routing platform; no programming language

standards.artifacts: None: data, platform vocabulary, prompts and code are proprietary (Data Availability section)

biases.detail: Authors evaluate their own system for their employer's platform on a benchmark they built, judged with a rulebook they pinned.
No data, schema, prompts or code are released, so no result can be replicated.
635 templated rules with 'manufactured synthetic data'; real administrator phrasing and production density are not measured.
One greedy run per cell; CIs are over items, not over sampling runs or prompt variants.
Opus 4.6 is both the judge and one of the generators; human agreement rests on a 22-item double-coded overlap.
The listing abstract presents ~89%/~90% 'across four models'; these are best-model figures, and the non-reasoning bridging claim fails for GPT-4.1.

coi.affiliations: Microsoft (all four authors, per email addresses; tables labelled 'Source: Microsoft')
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: The authors' own workflow-generation system for an unnamed commercial routing platform with a stated deployment path (§6); OpenAI and Anthropic models as backbones
coi.detail: A product feature evaluated by its builders on closed data with no independent replication. Severity is held at medium rather than high because the paper reports its own unfavourable results (GPT-4.1 no gain, ~8-point frontier gap, stubborn ordering errors).

verdict_reason: Paired same-model comparisons, McNemar and TOST tests, and candid negative results make the internal evidence reasonable. The caveats: everything is closed, it is a single run on templated synthetic data, the judge is also a generator, and the listing abstract inflates best-model numbers into cross-model ones. Admit as evidence that deterministic compilation of an LLM-emitted IR beats asking the model to emit a dense graph directly, for mid-tier models.
applicability: This is about generating a DAG as an output artifact, not about running the team's agents as a DAG. The transferable lesson applies wherever agents author graph-shaped config (ingestion pipeline definitions, Spring Batch or workflow-engine graphs, routing tables). Have the model emit a small IR and let deterministic Java code assemble and validate the graph, especially if cheaper non-reasoning models are used. For the team's DAG question it is a caution: even strong models get nodes right and edges wrong as interdependent nodes multiply, so any LLM-generated task DAG needs deterministic edge validation. It gives no evidence that a static workflow beats an open agent loop for multi-repo coding.

conflicts_with.detail: Tension: in DataFlow-Harness, making a strong model (Opus 4.7) build its deliverable as a typed DAG via validated mutations scored 83.3% vs 94.2% for writing scripts directly, whereas here routing a strong model through IR plus a compiler gains 4-5 pp. Targets, action spaces and the missing Skills arm differ, so this is not a direct contradiction.

Agree in direction: LoopsBench finds LLM plan DAGs reach only 0.27-0.71 edge F1 against reference DAGs; here edge-direction errors are 49.5% of residual failures. Both say models choose nodes better than they wire edges.
